NASB.1: I said to myself, 'Come now, I will test you with pleasure. So enjoy yourself.' And behold, it too was futility.
NASB.2: I said of laughter, 'It is madness,' and of pleasure, 'What does it accomplish?'
NASB.3: I explored with my mind [how] to stimulate my body with wine while my mind was guiding [me] wisely, and how to take hold of folly, until I could see what good there is for the sons of men to do under heaven the few years of their lives.
NASB.4: I enlarged my works: I built houses for myself, I planted vineyards for myself;
NASB.5: I made gardens and parks for myself and I planted in them all kinds of fruit trees;
NASB.6: I made ponds of water for myself from which to irrigate a forest of growing trees.
NASB.7: I bought male and female slaves and I had homeborn slaves. Also I possessed flocks and herds larger than all who preceded me in Jerusalem.
NASB.8: Also, I collected for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I provided for myself male and female singers and the pleasures of men-- many concubines.
NASB.9: Then I became great and increased more than all who preceded me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also stood by me.
NASB.10: All that my eyes desired I did not refuse them. I did not withhold my heart from any pleasure, for my heart was pleased because of all my labor and this was my reward for all my labor.
NASB.11: Thus I considered all my activities which my hands had done and the labor which I had exerted, and behold all was vanity and striving after wind and there was no profit under the sun.
NASB.12: So I turned to consider wisdom, madness and folly; for what [will] the man [do] who will come after the king [except] what has already been done?
NASB.13: And I saw that wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness.
NASB.14: The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I know that one fate befalls them both.
NASB.15: Then I said to myself, 'As is the fate of the fool, it will also befall me. Why then have I been extremely wise?' So I said to myself, 'This too is vanity.'
NASB.16: For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise man [as] with the fool, inasmuch as [in] the coming days all will be forgotten. And how the wise man and the fool alike die!
NASB.17: So I hated life, for the work which had been done under the sun was grievous to me; because everything is futility and striving after wind.
NASB.18: Thus I hated all the fruit of my labor for which I had labored under the sun, for I must leave it to the man who will come after me.
NASB.19: And who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have control over all the fruit of my labor for which I have labored by acting wisely under the sun. This too is vanity.
NASB.20: Therefore I completely despaired of all the fruit of my labor for which I had labored under the sun.
NASB.21: When there is a man who has labored with wisdom, knowledge and skill, then he gives his legacy to one who has not labored with them. This too is vanity and a great evil.
NASB.22: For what does a man get in all his labor and in his striving with which he labors under the sun?
NASB.23: Because all his days his task is painful and grievous; even at night his mind does not rest. This too is vanity.
NASB.24: There is nothing better for a man [than] to eat and drink and tell himself that his labor is good. This also I have seen that it is from the hand of God.
NASB.25: For who can eat and who can have enjoyment without Him?
NASB.26: For to a person who is good in His sight He has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, while to the sinner He has given the task of gathering and collecting so that he may give to one who is good in God's sight. This too is vanity and striving after wind.

ESV.1: I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself.” But behold, this also was vanity.
ESV.2: I said of laughter, “It is mad,” and of pleasure, “What use is it?”
ESV.3: I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine — my heart still guiding me with wisdom — and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.
ESV.4: I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself.
ESV.5: I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees.
ESV.6: I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees.
ESV.7: I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem.
ESV.8: I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines,  the delight of the sons of man.
ESV.9: So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me.
ESV.10: And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil.
ESV.11: Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
ESV.12: So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.
ESV.13: Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness.
ESV.14: The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them.
ESV.15: Then I said in my heart, “What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?” And I said in my heart that this also is vanity.
ESV.16: For of the wise as of the fool there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool!
ESV.17: So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.
ESV.18: I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me,
ESV.19: and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.
ESV.20: So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun,
ESV.21: because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.
ESV.22: What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun?
ESV.23: For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.
ESV.24: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment  in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God,
ESV.25: for apart from him  who can eat or who can have enjoyment?
ESV.26: For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.

NKJV.1: I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with mirth; therefore enjoy pleasure”; but surely, this also was vanity.
NKJV.2: I said of laughter—“Madness!”; and of mirth, “What does it accomplish?”
NKJV.3: I searched in my heart how to gratify my flesh with wine, while guiding my heart with wisdom, and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the sons of men to do under heaven all the days of their lives.
NKJV.4: I made my works great, I built myself houses, and planted myself vineyards.
NKJV.5: I made myself gardens and orchards, and I planted all kinds of fruit trees in them.
NKJV.6: I made myself water pools from which to water the growing trees of the grove.
NKJV.7: I acquired male and female servants, and had servants born in my house. Yes, I had greater possessions of herds and flocks than all who were in Jerusalem before me.
NKJV.8: I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the special treasures of kings and of the provinces. I acquired male and female singers, the delights of the sons of men, and musical instruments of all kinds.
NKJV.9: So I became great and excelled more than all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me.
NKJV.10: Whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I did not withhold my heart from any pleasure, For my heart rejoiced in all my labor; And this was my reward from all my labor.
NKJV.11: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had done And on the labor in which I had toiled; And indeed all was vanity and grasping for the wind. There was no profit under the sun.
NKJV.12: Then I turned myself to consider wisdom and madness and folly; For what can the man do who succeeds the king?— Only what he has already done.
NKJV.13: Then I saw that wisdom excels folly As light excels darkness.
NKJV.14: The wise man’s eyes are in his head, But the fool walks in darkness. Yet I myself perceived That the same event happens to them all.
NKJV.15: So I said in my heart, “As it happens to the fool, It also happens to me, And why was I then more wise?” Then I said in my heart, “This also is vanity.”
NKJV.16: For there is no more remembrance of the wise than of the fool forever, Since all that now is will be forgotten in the days to come. And how does a wise man die? As the fool!
NKJV.17: Therefore I hated life because the work that was done under the sun was distressing to me, for all is vanity and grasping for the wind.
NKJV.18: Then I hated all my labor in which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who will come after me.
NKJV.19: And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will rule over all my labor in which I toiled and in which I have shown myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
NKJV.20: Therefore I turned my heart and despaired of all the labor in which I had toiled under the sun.
NKJV.21: For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, knowledge, and skill; yet he must leave his heritage to a man who has not labored for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.
NKJV.22: For what has man for all his labor, and for the striving of his heart with which he has toiled under the sun?
NKJV.23: For all his days are sorrowful, and his work burdensome; even in the night his heart takes no rest. This also is vanity.
NKJV.24: Nothing is better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and that his soul should enjoy good in his labor. This also, I saw, was from the hand of God.
NKJV.25: For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?
NKJV.26: For God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy to a man who is good in His sight; but to the sinner He gives the work of gathering and collecting, that he may give to him who is good before God. This also is vanity and grasping for the wind.

AMP.1: I said to myself, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure and gratification; so enjoy yourself and have a good time." But behold, this too was vanity (futility, meaninglessness).
AMP.2: I said of laughter, "It is madness," and of pleasure, "What does it accomplish?"
AMP.3: I explored with my mind how to gratify myself with wine while [at the same time] having my mind remain steady and guide me wisely; and how to take control of foolishness, until I could see what was good for the sons of men to do under heaven all the days of their lives.
AMP.4: I made great works: I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards for myself;
AMP.5: I made gardens and orchards for myself and I planted in them all kinds of fruit trees;
AMP.6: I made pools of water for myself from which to water the forest and make the trees bud.
AMP.7: I bought male and female slaves and had slaves born in my house. I also possessed herds and flocks larger than any who preceded me in Jerusalem.
AMP.8: Also, I collected for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I provided for myself male singers and female singers, and the delights and pleasures of men— many concubines.
AMP.9: So I became great and excelled more than all who preceded me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also remained with me.
AMP.10: Whatever my eyes looked at with desire I did not refuse them. I did not withhold from my heart any pleasure, for my heart was pleased because of all my labor; and this was my reward for all my labor.
AMP.11: Then I considered all which my hands had done and labored to do, and behold, all was vanity and chasing after the wind and there was no profit (nothing of lasting value) under the sun.
AMP.12: So I turned to consider [secular] wisdom, madness, and folly; for what will the man do who succeeds the king? Nothing except what has already been done.
AMP.13: Then I saw that [even secular] wisdom [that brings sorrow] is better than [the pleasures of] folly and self-indulgence as light excels darkness.
AMP.14: The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness; and yet I know that [in the end] one fate happens to them both.
AMP.15: Then I said to myself, "As it happens to the fool, so death will also happen to me. What use is it then for me to be extremely wise?" Then I said in my heart, "This too is vanity (meaningless)."
AMP.16: For there is no [more] lasting remembrance of the wise man than of the fool, since in the days to come all will be long forgotten. And how does the wise man die? Even as the fool!
AMP.17: So I hated life, for the work which had been done under the sun caused me only great sorrow; because all is futility and chasing after the wind.
AMP.18: So I hated all the fruit (gain) of my labor for which I had labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who will succeed me.
AMP.19: And who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have control over all the fruit of my labor for which I have labored by acting wisely under the sun. This too is vanity (futility, self-conceit).
AMP.20: So I turned aside and let my heart despair over all the fruit of my labor for which I had labored under the sun.
AMP.21: For there is a man who has labored with wisdom and knowledge and skill, yet gives his legacy to one who has not labored for it. This too is vanity and a great evil.
AMP.22: For what does a man get from all his labor and from the striving and sorrow of his heart with which he labors under the sun?
AMP.23: For all his days his work is painful and sorrowful; even at night his mind does not rest. This too is vanity (worthless).
AMP.24: There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink and assure himself that there is good in his labor. Even this, I have seen, is from the hand of God.
AMP.25: For who can eat and who can have enjoyment without Him?
AMP.26: For to the person who pleases Him God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner He gives the work of gathering and collecting so that he may give to one who pleases God. This too is vanity and chasing after the wind.

CSB17.16: For, just like the fool, there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, <sup>ⓖ</sup> since in the days to come both will be forgotten. How is it that the wise person dies just like the fool?
CSB17.17: Therefore, I hated life because the work that was done under the sun was distressing to me. For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
CSB17.18: I hated all my work that I labored at under the sun <sup>ⓗ</sup> because I must leave it to the one who comes after me. <sup>ⓘ</sup>
CSB17.19: And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? <sup>ⓙ</sup> Yet he will take over all my work that I labored at skillfully under the sun. This too is futile.
CSB17.20: So I began to give myself over <sup>[8]</sup> to despair concerning all my work that I had labored at under the sun.
CSB17.21: When there is a person whose work was done with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, <sup>ⓚ</sup> and he must give his portion to a person who has not worked for it, this too is futile and a great wrong.
CSB17.22: For what does a person get with all his work and all his efforts <sup>ⓛ</sup> that he labors at under the sun?
CSB17.23: For all his days are filled with grief, and his occupation is sorrowful; <sup>ⓜ</sup> even at night, his mind does not rest. <sup>ⓝ</sup> This too is futile.
CSB17.24: There is nothing better for a person than to eat, drink, and enjoy <sup>[9]</sup> <sup>[10]</sup> his work. <sup>ⓐ</sup> I have seen that even this is from God’s hand, <sup>ⓑ</sup>
CSB17.25: because who can eat and who can enjoy life <sup>[11]</sup> apart from him? <sup>[12]</sup>
CSB17.26: For to the person who is pleasing in his sight, he gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; <sup>ⓒ</sup> but to the sinner he gives the task of gathering and accumulating in order to give to the one who is pleasing in God’s sight. <sup>ⓓ</sup> This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind. <sup>ⓔ</sup>

WEB.1: I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with mirth: therefore enjoy pleasure”; and behold, this also was vanity.
WEB.2: I said of laughter, “It is foolishness”; and of mirth, “What does it accomplish?”
WEB.3: I searched in my heart how to cheer my flesh with wine, my heart yet guiding me with wisdom, and how to lay hold of folly, until I might see what it was good for the sons of men that they should do under heaven all the days of their lives.
WEB.4: I made myself great works. I built myself houses. I planted myself vineyards.
WEB.5: I made myself gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of all kinds of fruit.
WEB.6: I made myself pools of water, to water from it the forest where trees were reared.
WEB.7: I bought male servants and female servants, and had servants born in my house. I also had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all who were before me in Jerusalem;
WEB.8: I also gathered silver and gold for myself, and the treasure of kings and of the provinces. I got myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men — musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
WEB.9: So I was great, and increased more than all who were before me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also remained with me.
WEB.10: Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.
WEB.11: Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
WEB.12: I turned myself to consider wisdom, madness, and folly: for what can the king’s successor do? Just that which has been done long ago.
WEB.13: Then I saw that wisdom excels folly, as far as light excels darkness.
WEB.14: The wise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool walks in darkness — and yet I perceived that one event happens to them all.
WEB.15: Then I said in my heart, “As it happens to the fool, so will it happen even to me; and why was I then more wise?” Then I said in my heart that this also is vanity.
WEB.16: For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no memory for ever, since in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. Indeed, the wise man must die just like the fool!
WEB.17: So I hated life, because the work that is worked under the sun was grievous to me; for all is vanity and a chasing after wind.
WEB.18: I hated all my labor in which I labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
WEB.19: Who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have rule over all of my labor in which I have labored, and in which I have shown myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
WEB.20: Therefore I began to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor in which I had labored under the sun.
WEB.21: For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, with knowledge, and with skillfulness; yet he shall leave it for his portion to a man who has not labored for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.
WEB.22: For what has a man of all his labor, and of the striving of his heart, in which he labors under the sun?
WEB.23: For all his days are sorrows, and his travail is grief; yes, even in the night his heart takes no rest. This also is vanity.
WEB.24: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
WEB.25: For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?
WEB.26: For to the man who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he gives travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him who pleases God. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

NLT.1: I said to myself, “Come on, let’s try pleasure. Let’s look for the ‘good things’ in life.” But I found that this, too, was meaningless.
NLT.2: So I said, “Laughter is silly. What good does it do to seek pleasure?”
NLT.3: After much thought, I decided to cheer myself with wine. And while still seeking wisdom, I clutched at foolishness. In this way, I tried to experience the only happiness most people find during their brief life in this world.
NLT.4: I also tried to find meaning by building huge homes for myself and by planting beautiful vineyards.
NLT.5: I made gardens and parks, filling them with all kinds of fruit trees.
NLT.6: I built reservoirs to collect the water to irrigate my many flourishing groves.
NLT.7: I bought slaves, both men and women, and others were born into my household. I also owned large herds and flocks, more than any of the kings who had lived in Jerusalem before me.
NLT.8: I collected great sums of silver and gold, the treasure of many kings and provinces. I hired wonderful singers, both men and women, and had many beautiful concubines. I had everything a man could desire!
NLT.9: So I became greater than all who had lived in Jerusalem before me, and my wisdom never failed me.
NLT.10: Anything I wanted, I would take. I denied myself no pleasure. I even found great pleasure in hard work, a reward for all my labors.
NLT.11: But as I looked at everything I had worked so hard to accomplish, it was all so meaningless — like chasing the wind. There was nothing really worthwhile anywhere.
NLT.12: So I decided to compare wisdom with foolishness and madness (for who can do this better than I, the king? ).
NLT.13: I thought, “Wisdom is better than foolishness, just as light is better than darkness.
NLT.14: For the wise can see where they are going, but fools walk in the dark.” Yet I saw that the wise and the foolish share the same fate.
NLT.15: Both will die. So I said to myself, “Since I will end up the same as the fool, what’s the value of all my wisdom? This is all so meaningless!”
NLT.16: For the wise and the foolish both die. The wise will not be remembered any longer than the fool. In the days to come, both will be forgotten.
NLT.17: So I came to hate life because everything done here under the sun is so troubling. Everything is meaningless — like chasing the wind.
NLT.18: I came to hate all my hard work here on earth, for I must leave to others everything I have earned.
NLT.19: And who can tell whether my successors will be wise or foolish? Yet they will control everything I have gained by my skill and hard work under the sun. How meaningless!
NLT.20: So I gave up in despair, questioning the value of all my hard work in this world.
NLT.21: Some people work wisely with knowledge and skill, then must leave the fruit of their efforts to someone who hasn’t worked for it. This, too, is meaningless, a great tragedy.
NLT.22: So what do people get in this life for all their hard work and anxiety?
NLT.23: Their days of labor are filled with pain and grief; even at night their minds cannot rest. It is all meaningless.
NLT.24: So I decided there is nothing better than to enjoy food and drink and to find satisfaction in work. Then I realized that these pleasures are from the hand of God.
NLT.25: For who can eat or enjoy anything apart from him?
NLT.26: God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please him. But if a sinner becomes wealthy, God takes the wealth away and gives it to those who please him. This, too, is meaningless — like chasing the wind.

MSG.1: I said to myself, "Let's go for it—experiment with pleasure, have a good time!" But there was nothing to it, nothing but smoke.
MSG.2:
What do I think of the fun-filled life? Insane! Inane!
My verdict on the pursuit of happiness? Who needs it?
MSG.3:
With the help of a bottle of wine
and all the wisdom I could muster,
I tried my level best
to penetrate the absurdity of life.
I wanted to get a handle on anything useful we mortals might do
during the years we spend on this earth.
MSG.4:
Oh, I did great things:
built houses,
planted vineyards,
MSG.5:
designed gardens and parks
and planted a variety of fruit trees in them,
MSG.6:
made pools of water
to irrigate the groves of trees.
MSG.7:
I bought slaves, male and female,
who had children, giving me even more slaves;
then I acquired large herds and flocks,
larger than any before me in Jerusalem.
MSG.8:
I piled up silver and gold,
loot from kings and kingdoms.
I gathered a chorus of singers to entertain me with song,
and—most exquisite of all pleasures—
voluptuous maidens for my bed.
MSG.9: Oh, how I prospered! I left all my predecessors in Jerusalem far behind, left them behind in the dust. What's more, I kept a clear head through it all.
MSG.10: Everything I wanted I took—I never said no to myself. I gave in to every impulse, held back nothing. I sucked the marrow of pleasure out of every task—my reward to myself for a hard day's work!
MSG.11: Then I took a good look at everything I'd done, looked at all the sweat and hard work. But when I looked, I saw nothing but smoke. Smoke and spitting into the wind. There was nothing to any of it. Nothing.
MSG.12: And then I took a hard look at what's smart and what's stupid. What's left to do after you've been king? That's a hard act to follow. You just do what you can, and that's it.
MSG.13: But I did see that it's better to be smart than stupid, just as light is better than darkness.
MSG.14: Even so, though the smart ones see where they're going and the stupid ones grope in the dark, they're all the same in the end. One fate for all—and that's it.
MSG.15: When I realized that my fate's the same as the fool's, I had to ask myself, "So why bother being wise?" It's all smoke, nothing but smoke.
MSG.16: The smart and the stupid both disappear out of sight. In a day or two they're both forgotten. Yes, both the smart and the stupid die, and that's it.
MSG.17: I hate life. As far as I can see, what happens on earth is a bad business. It's smoke—and spitting into the wind.
MSG.18: And I hated everything I'd accomplished and accumulated on this earth. I can't take it with me—no, I have to leave it to whoever comes after me.
MSG.19: Whether they're worthy or worthless—and who's to tell?—they'll take over the earthly results of my intense thinking and hard work. Smoke.
MSG.20: That's when I called it quits, gave up on anything that could be hoped for on this earth.
MSG.21: What's the point of working your fingers to the bone if you hand over what you worked for to someone who never lifted a finger for it? Smoke, that's what it is. A bad business from start to finish.
MSG.22: So what do you get from a life of hard labor?
MSG.23: Pain and grief from dawn to dusk. Never a decent night's rest. Nothing but smoke.
MSG.24: The best you can do with your life is have a good time and get by the best you can. The way I see it, that's it—divine fate.
MSG.25: Whether we feast or fast, it's up to God.
MSG.26: God may give wisdom and knowledge and joy to his favorites, but sinners are assigned a life of hard labor, and end up turning their wages over to God's favorites. Nothing but smoke—and spitting into the wind.

NIV.1:
Pleasures Are Meaningless
I thought in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with pleasure to find out what is good.” But that also proved to be meaningless.
NIV.2: “Laughter,” I said, “is foolish. And what does pleasure accomplish?”
NIV.3: I tried cheering myself with wine, and embracing folly—my mind still guiding me with wisdom. I wanted to see what was worthwhile for men to do under heaven during the few days of their lives.
NIV.4: I undertook great projects: I built houses for myself and planted vineyards.
NIV.5: I made gardens and parks and planted all kinds of fruit trees in them.
NIV.6: I made reservoirs to water groves of flourishing trees.
NIV.7: I bought male and female slaves and had other slaves who were born in my house. I also owned more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before me.
NIV.8: I amassed silver and gold for myself, and the treasure of kings and provinces. I acquired men and women singers, and a harem as well—the delights of the heart of man.
NIV.9: I became greater by far than anyone in Jerusalem before me. In all this my wisdom stayed with me.
NIV.10:
I denied myself nothing my eyes desired;
I refused my heart no pleasure.
My heart took delight in all my work,
and this was the reward for all my labor.
NIV.11:
Yet when I surveyed all that my hands had done
and what I had toiled to achieve,
everything was meaningless, a chasing after the wind;
nothing was gained under the sun.
NIV.12:
Wisdom and Folly Are Meaningless
Then I turned my thoughts to consider wisdom,
and also madness and folly.
What more can the king’s successor do
than what has already been done?
NIV.13:
I saw that wisdom is better than folly,
just as light is better than darkness.
NIV.14:
The wise man has eyes in his head,
while the fool walks in the darkness;
but I came to realize
that the same fate overtakes them both.
NIV.15:
Then I thought in my heart,
“The fate of the fool will overtake me also.
What then do I gain by being wise?”

NIV.16:
For the wise man, like the fool, will not be long remembered;
in days to come both will be forgotten.

NIV.17:
Toil Is Meaningless
So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. All of it is meaningless, a chasing after the wind.
NIV.18: I hated all the things I had toiled for under the sun, because I must leave them to the one who comes after me.
NIV.19: And who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have control over all the work into which I have poured my effort and skill under the sun. This too is meaningless.
NIV.20: So my heart began to despair over all my toilsome labor under the sun.
NIV.21: For a man may do his work with wisdom, knowledge and skill, and then he must leave all he owns to someone who has not worked for it. This too is meaningless and a great misfortune.

NET.1: I thought to myself, “Come now, I will try self-indulgent pleasure to see if it is worthwhile.” But I found that it also is futile.
NET.2: I said of partying, “It is folly,” and of self-indulgent pleasure, “It accomplishes nothing!”
NET.3: I thought deeply about the effects of indulging myself with wine (all the while my mind was guiding me with wisdom) and the effects of behaving foolishly, so that I might discover what is profitable for people to do on earth during the few days of their lives.
NET.4: I increased my possessions: I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards for myself.
NET.5: I designed royal gardens and parks for myself, and I planted all kinds of fruit trees in them.
NET.6: I constructed pools of water for myself, to irrigate my grove of flourishing trees.
NET.7: I purchased male and female slaves, and I owned slaves who were born in my house; I also possessed more livestock — both herds and flocks — than any of my predecessors in Jerusalem.
NET.8: I also amassed silver and gold for myself, as well as valuable treasures taken from kingdoms and provinces. I acquired male singers and female singers for myself, and what gives a man sensual delight — a harem of beautiful concubines!
NET.9: So I was far wealthier than all my predecessors in Jerusalem, yet I maintained my objectivity:
NET.10: I did not restrain myself from getting whatever I wanted; I did not deny myself anything that would bring me pleasure. So all my accomplishments gave me joy; this was my reward for all my effort.
NET.11: Yet when I reflected on everything I had accomplished and on all the effort that I had expended to accomplish it, I concluded: “All these achievements and possessions are ultimately profitless — like chasing the wind! There is nothing gained from them on earth.”
NET.12: Next, I decided to consider wisdom, as well as foolish behavior and ideas. For what more can the king’s successor do than what the king has already done?
NET.13: I realized that wisdom is preferable to folly, just as light is preferable to darkness:
NET.14: The wise man can see where he is going, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also realized that the same fate happens to them both.
NET.15: So I thought to myself, “The fate of the fool will happen even to me! Then what did I gain by becoming so excessively wise?” So I lamented to myself, “The benefits of wisdom are ultimately meaningless!”
NET.16: For the wise man, like the fool, will not be remembered for very long, because in the days to come, both will already have been forgotten. Alas, the wise man dies — just like the fool!
NET.17: So I loathed life because what happens on earth seems awful to me; for all the benefits of wisdom are futile — like chasing the wind.
NET.18: So I loathed all the fruit of my effort, for which I worked so hard on earth, because I must leave it behind in the hands of my successor.
NET.19: Who knows if he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will be master over all the fruit of my labor for which I worked so wisely on earth! This also is futile!
NET.20: So I began to despair about all the fruit of my labor for which I worked so hard on earth.
NET.21: For a man may do his work with wisdom, knowledge, and skill; however, he must hand over the fruit of his labor as an inheritance to someone else who did not work for it. This also is futile, and an awful injustice!
NET.22: What does a man acquire from all his labor and from the anxiety that accompanies his toil on earth?
NET.23: For all day long his work produces pain and frustration, and even at night his mind cannot relax! This also is futile!
NET.24: There is nothing better for people than to eat and drink, and to find enjoyment in their work. I also perceived that this ability to find enjoyment comes from God.
NET.25: For no one can eat and drink or experience joy apart from him.
NET.26: For to the one who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy, but to the sinner, he gives the task of amassing wealth — only to give it to the one who pleases God. This task of the wicked is futile — like chasing the wind!
